title: Lesson 78: Workflow Engines vs Agents: When to Use Deterministic Orchestration
description: Separating code-controlled workflows from model-controlled agents, what durable execution actually guarantees, applying the five-question test, and placing one bounded agentic step inside a deterministic skeleton.

questions.question: A team is automating a document intake process. The steps are always the same, the number of documents varies by batch, and every extraction output can be checked against a JSON schema. Per the lesson's five-question test, what shape should they build?
options: An autonomous agent, because the document count varies and the model should decide how many to read
An orchestrator-workers system with no fixed outer structure, so subtasks can be discovered per batch
A workflow, because the steps are enumerable, the step count is bounded by the batch, and a validator can decide whether each step succeeded
A workflow only if the model is removed entirely, since any model call inside durable code breaks determinism
questions.explanation: The lesson scores enumerability, bounded step count, and validator-gated success as workflow answers, and warns that a wrong branch is what pushes toward code-controlled paths. It also states the model may do real work inside a workflow, but never chooses the next step.

questions.question: In the contract renewal worked example, the agent-shaped version produced three problems: skipped documents, ungated extraction flowing into a recommendation, and a bill that varied by a factor of three. What does the lesson identify as the root cause?
options: The model was too small for the task, so extraction quality collapsed without control
The agent was doing what agents do, deciding, when the design never said which decisions were its to make; the fix is moving it to the exception queue where judgment pays
The tools were misconfigured, so the agent could not see two of the forty documents
The workflow engine's retry policy was missing, which caused the cost variance across runs
questions.explanation: The lesson frames all three as controls that were removed rather than a worse model, and prescribes moving the agent to the rung where its judgment adds value: the exception queue, where the path genuinely varies and a person checks the output.

questions.question: You want an agent to run as one step inside a durable workflow. Which seam contract does the lesson require before the first run?
options: Let the agent write directly to the workflow's event history so the engine can replay its reasoning later
Give the agent an unbounded iteration budget so it can always finish, and log the transcript for audit
Call the model directly from the deterministic workflow body so the engine can cache the result on replay
A typed input schema, a typed output schema, validation at the boundary, an idempotency key, a timeout, a cost ceiling, and a defined escalation when validation fails
questions.explanation: The lesson lists exactly those seven items as the seam contract and warns that every undefined one becomes an incident. It also warns that a model call inside deterministic workflow code returns a different answer on replay and breaks the history match.
